analysis.one_liner: Lets workers on strike collect unemployment benefits after two weeks off the job.
analysis.headline: A bill to pay unemployment benefits to striking workers drew 60 House cosponsors, all Democrats, but never got a hearing or a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Today, workers who walk off the job in a strike generally cannot collect unemployment insurance, because they are not considered unemployed and are usually disqualified as strikers. This bill would change federal law so striking workers — and workers idled indirectly by a strike or lockout — can receive unemployment benefits starting 14 days after a strike begins, immediately after a lockout, or when the employer hires permanent replacements. It would also exempt them from the usual rules that they be available for work and actively job-hunting while collecting. The bill was sent to the tax-writing House Ways and Means Committee and never moved.
analysis.who_benefits: Striking workers and their families, who would keep receiving an income during a strike instead of going weeks or months without pay. Workers at suppliers or other businesses shut down indirectly by a labor dispute would also qualify. Unions gain bargaining leverage, because members could hold out longer without falling behind on rent and groceries.

how_it_helps.text: Allows a worker unable to work because of a labor dispute to be treated as unemployed and receive unemployment compensation, starting 14 days after a strike begins, when a lockout starts, or when the employer hires permanent replacement workers.
Covers workers idled as an indirect result of a labor dispute, not just the strikers themselves, so employees of affected suppliers or customers can qualify too.
Exempts these workers from the federal requirement that unemployment claimants be available for work and actively seeking work while they collect benefits.
Would let a locked-out worker collect from day one, since the bill pays benefits when a lockout begins, unlike the 14-day wait that applies to strikers.

analysis.who_pays: State unemployment insurance funds, which would pay the new claims, and employers, who generally repay the system through experience-rated payroll taxes — meaning employers whose workers strike would effectively help finance the benefits. Supporters argue this rebalances a bargaining table where employers can simply wait out workers; opponents say it turns unemployment insurance, meant for people who lose jobs involuntarily, into strike funding.

drawbacks.text: Unemployment insurance is funded by state taxes on employers, so the bill would add strike payrolls to those funds and could raise costs for the employers involved, costs that can be passed on in prices.

Critics of paying strikers argue that unemployment insurance is designed for workers who lose their jobs through no choice of their own, and that a strike is a voluntary withholding of labor; the bill treats a striker as though unemployed, which changes the program's purpose.

Because benefits would make long strikes easier to sustain, opponents warn it could lengthen work stoppages, which also hurts the communities and businesses around a struck plant — though the bill's 14-day waiting period for strikers is a partial answer to that concern.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and targeted: workers on strike now face the harshest possible cash squeeze, with no paycheck and, in most states, no benefits, which pushes many to cave quickly even when they have a strong case. The costs are modest relative to that — state UI funds already handle layoffs and are partly experience-rated so the employers in a dispute bear much of the charge. The honest objection is philosophical: this redefines unemployment insurance to cover a chosen work stoppage, and the bill includes no dedicated funding. As drafted, it is a straightforward income floor for striking workers with a reasonable waiting period, and the main design gap is that it leaves states to absorb the cost.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced, later passed to a subcommittee, and never received a hearing or a vote before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Adam Schiff introduced the bill on October 25, 2023, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means, the committee with jurisdiction over unemployment insurance.
Sixty House members cosponsored the bill — all Democrats — including Reps. Ocasio-Cortez, Khanna, Jayapal, and others.
On December 17, 2024, more than a year after introduction, the bill was referred to the Subcommittee on Work and Welfare — a late, low-level step that typically signals no committee action is coming.
The bill never received a committee markup, a floor vote, or any Senate companion action, and died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers facing strikes are better off, since the bargaining leverage this bill would have handed to workers never materialized. Striking workers are no better off than before: in most states they still cannot collect unemployment benefits during a labor dispute.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers facing strikes and their allies

for.name: Rep. Adam Schiff
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to let striking workers collect unemployment benefits.

for.name: 59 House cosponsors
for.role: All Democrats, including Ocasio-Cortez, Khanna, Jayapal, Norcross, and Casar
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, giving the bill 60 supporters in the House.

against.name: Rep. Jason Smith
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: His committee took no action on the bill — no markup or hearing — after it was referred on the day of introduction.

against.name: House Republican majority
against.role: Majority party controlling the House floor and committee agendas in the 118th Congress
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a floor vote during two years in which it controlled what came to the floor.

sides.party_line_note: All 60 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican cosponsored, and the Republican-run Ways and Means Committee never acted on it.

industries.note: The bill would undercut an employer's ability to wait out a strike, since workers would draw benefits after two weeks rather than running out of money. Its death preserves the current leverage employers hold in negotiations.
Union members would keep an income during strikes, and unions could sustain work stoppages longer. The bill's failure leaves unions negotiating without that safety net.

States would administer and pay new classes of claims, expanding the program's reach while adding costs without dedicated new funding. Most of the burden would flow back to employers through experience-rated taxes.
